opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the core question behind a lot of the work we've been doing on joint-embedding predictive architectures, like I-JEPA and V-JEPA.

If your goal is just to generate realistic images or video, then of course you care about every pixel. But if your goal is to understand the world well enough to reason and plan, then much of that detail is a distraction. Think about the exact texture of leaves on a tree, or the precise pattern of ripples on water. Those things are fundamentally unpredictable, and they're also mostly irrelevant to what you'd need to make a decision. A model trained to reconstruct pixels has to spend a huge amount of its capacity and compute trying to predict that kind of low-level, high-entropy detail. You end up paying a lot for information that doesn't help downstream.

So the way we approach it is to make predictions in a learned representation space instead of in pixel space. The model gets to learn an abstract representation where it can throw away the unpredictable or irrelevant details, and focus on predicting the things that are actually predictable and semantically meaningful, like where objects are, how they move, how they interact.

As for how we actually judge efficiency, there are a few angles. One is sample and compute efficiency in pretraining. We've consistently seen that predicting in latent space gets you to strong representations with fewer GPU hours and often fewer samples than pixel-reconstruction approaches like masked autoencoders. Another is the quality of the representations under frozen evaluation. If you freeze the backbone and train only a lightweight probe on top, how well does it do on things like action recognition, motion understanding, or object-level tasks? That tells you whether the model captured something semantic, or just learned to paint in details. And increasingly the most important test is downstream use in planning. Can you take that representation, train a predictor conditioned on actions, and then use it to plan in a robot setting, zero-shot, without having ever seen task-specific rewards? If the latent space is good, planning becomes a lot cheaper because you're searching over compact, meaningful states rather than over high-dimensional images.

That said, I don't think it's a completely solved trade-off. Sometimes the fine details do matter. If you're doing precise manipulation, small geometric details can be critical. So part of the research question is how to learn representations that are abstract enough to be efficient, but still retain whatever detail is necessary for the task. Ideally the model learns that hierarchy itself: coarse abstractions for long-horizon reasoning, and finer-grained information when you need it for short-horizon control.

r001.rationale: The response says pixel reconstruction spends substantial capacity and compute on unpredictable, mostly irrelevant details that do not help reasoning or decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really the crux of it. If you look at the dominant paradigm in generative modeling, the idea is that you train a model to predict every pixel, or every token of a video, and the hope is that in doing so it will implicitly learn everything about the world. And in some sense that's true, you'll learn a lot. But the question is whether that's the efficient path to the thing you actually care about, which is understanding, reasoning, and planning.

And my view is that it's not. Most of the information content in a video, if you measure it in bits, is stuff that's fundamentally unpredictable and also irrelevant for planning. The exact texture of the leaves on a tree when the wind blows, the precise pattern of ripples on water, the noise in the sensor. If you force a model to spend its capacity modeling all of that, you're paying a huge computational cost for details that don't help you decide what to do next. A person doesn't predict every pixel of the room before they reach for a cup of coffee. They have an abstract representation of where the cup is, roughly what will happen when they grab it, and that's enough.

So the way I judge efficiency is: how much compute, how much data, do you need to get a representation that supports the downstream task? And that's really the motivation behind the joint-embedding predictive architecture work, JEPA. Instead of predicting in pixel space, you predict in representation space. The model learns an encoder, and the prediction task is to predict the representation of the missing or future part of the input from the representation of what you've seen. The nice property is that the encoder is free to throw away information. It can learn to discard the unpredictable, high-entropy stuff and keep the things that are actually predictable and semantically meaningful.

Now, there's an obvious objection, which is that if the encoder can throw away information, why doesn't it throw away everything and just collapse to a constant? That's the real technical challenge with these methods, and a lot of the work is about how you design the objective and the architecture so that you avoid collapse while still getting that selective abstraction. But when you do get it right, what you see empirically is that these models learn useful representations with a lot less compute than the pixel-reconstruction approaches, and they're much better at the things that look like understanding. Can you tell whether a scene is physically plausible, can you predict roughly what happens next at a semantic level, can you use the representation to plan actions for a robot.

So I'd say efficiency isn't about how many bits of the input you can reproduce. It's about how cheaply you arrive at the abstractions that let you act in the world. And by that measure, modeling every detail is often the wrong objective.

r001.rationale: The response says modeling every pixel spends substantial capacity and compute on unpredictable details irrelevant to planning, making it an inefficient path to understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you want the model to do. If your goal is to generate an image, then modeling every visual detail makes sense. But if your goal is to understand what’s happening and predict the consequences of an action, a lot of those details may be irrelevant.

Imagine watching an object move across a table. For planning, you care about where it is, how it’s moving, and what happens if you push it. You probably don’t need to predict the exact texture of the table or how the lighting changes at every pixel. Modeling all of that can be expensive, and it asks the model to solve a harder problem than the one you actually care about.

So the idea is to predict in a representation space, where you can retain the information that matters without reconstructing every detail. The challenge is learning that abstraction: you want to discard things that are unpredictable or irrelevant, while preserving enough information to support reasoning and planning.

r001.rationale: The response says that modeling irrelevant visual details for understanding and planning can be expensive and makes the model solve a harder problem than needed, then recommends retaining only useful information in a representation space. This communicates the inefficiency of spending model resources on every visual detail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you want the model to do. If your goal is to generate an image, then modeling all those visual details matters. But if your goal is to understand what’s happening and plan an action, a lot of those details are irrelevant. You don’t necessarily need to predict the texture of a table to know that an object placed on it will stay there.

So the question is: can we learn a representation that preserves the information needed for reasoning and prediction, without spending capacity on every pixel? That’s the motivation for predicting in representation space. You want to capture the underlying structure of the world while abstracting away details that are difficult to predict and don’t affect the decision you’re trying to make. Of course, the challenge is learning what to keep and what to discard.

r001.rationale: The response says many visual details are irrelevant to understanding and planning and motivates abstracting them away to avoid spending capacity on every pixel.
